The Ohio River. A major tributary of the Mississippi River, the Ohio flows approximately nine hundred eighty miles from Pennsylvania to Kentucky, draining the Appalachian region and industrial heartland of America. It formed the traditional boundary between the Ohio River Valley's northern settlement and the southern frontier during American expansion. The river originates at the confluence of the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where tributaries flow out of the Appalachian highlands. Historically it marked the northern limit of southern slavery in pre-Civil War America, serving as a geographic and cultural boundary between north and south. The Ohio flows through or borders West Virginia, Kentucky, Indiana, and Illinois, serving major industrial cities including Pittsburgh, Cincinnati, and Louisville. The name comes from the Iroquoian word O-hi-yo, meaning great river or great water. The river provides hydroelectric power, barge transportation, and water supply for millions of people in the upper Mississippi Valley and Ohio Valley regions. It forms a major transportation corridor with a series of locks and dams that allow commercial navigation despite natural rapids and falls. The Ohio River Flooding of nineteen thirty-seven was one of the worst natural disasters in American history, inundating entire communities along its banks. As the primary eastern tributary, it joins the Mississippi vastly expanding the downstream flow.
